statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether rates of schizophrenia or psychosis changed as cannabis use rose: the studies that narrative reviews cite disagree, all are ecological, and their figures are second-hand here. As described in two reviews, an Australian modelling study by the reviewers' own group found no clear rise in psychosis incidence after steep rises in cannabis use in the 1980s and 1990s; a British modelling study judged it too early to see any rise in England and Wales; case-register studies in Britain and Switzerland (south-east London and Zurich) reported rising incidence of psychoses in recent birth cohorts; and a British study of people treated for schizophrenia in general practice found no increase, cited to a 2008 government advisory report (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015). Another review describes incidence of schizophrenia in south-east London as doubling between 1965 and 1999 while the share of patients who had used cannabis rose (Murray et al., 2016), and a third cites a 2009 paper on diagnosed schizophrenia in the UK from 1996 to 2005 among studies finding no change or a decrease (Gage et al., 2016). A critical overview states that UK cannabis use rose at least tenfold since the 1970s, citing a commentary for this, and that first admissions for schizophrenia did not rise and perhaps fell slightly, without a source for the admissions figures, and treats this as evidence against a causal effect (Ksir & Hart, 2016). Reviews that lean towards a causal reading call such evidence weak: it cannot show that the people who used cannabis are those who became ill, and it does not account for confounders or for other risk factors that may have fallen over the same period (Gage et al., 2016); even a causal effect would raise incidence only modestly, and changes in diagnostic criteria and services, poor administrative data and possible falls in incidence from social improvements could hide a rise (Hall, 2015). The 2007 systematic review cites the same Australian and British modelling studies rather than new data (Moore et al., 2007), and a 2021 viewpoint calls for controlled before-and-after comparisons where cannabis use rose after decriminalization (Gillespie & Kendler, 2021). Across places rather than over time, in one primary study of 10 sites in Europe and Brazil, adjusted incidence of psychotic disorder was higher where more controls reported daily use (r about 0.8) or high-potency use (about 0.7); this is an ecological correlation, and although the paper calls the two measures only modestly correlated (r = 0.2), its own site figures correlate at about 0.71 (editors' calculation), so the two correlations are not separate evidence (Di Forti et al., 2019). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: If cannabis causes psychosis, rates of schizophrenia might be expected to rise when more people use cannabis. The studies that reviews describe disagree: an Australian study found no clear rise after cannabis use went up, studies in south-east London and Zurich found psychosis becoming more common in people born more recently, and a review says that in the UK first hospital admissions for schizophrenia did not rise although cannabis use rose at least tenfold. These studies compare whole populations over time, so they cannot tell whether the people who used cannabis are the ones who became ill, and changes in how illness is diagnosed and recorded could hide a rise. They are known here only through reviews.
population: Whole populations over time in Australia, England and Wales, south-east London, Zurich and the UK, as described in narrative reviews; and 10 catchment areas in the UK, the Netherlands, France, Spain, Italy and Brazil compared with each other (2010 to 2015)
exposure: Rising cannabis use in the population over decades (as described in the reviews); across sites, the share of population controls reporting daily or high-potency use
comparator: Earlier periods or birth cohorts in the same populations; sites with less daily or high-potency use
outcome: Incidence of schizophrenia or psychotic disorder (treated or registered cases, first admissions, modelled incidence); across sites, adjusted incidence of psychotic disorder per 100,000 person-years
magnitude: No pooled estimate. As described in reviews: no clear rise in Australia (modelling); too early to detect in England and Wales (modelling); rising incidence in recent birth cohorts in south-east London and Zurich (case registers), with schizophrenia incidence in south-east London described as doubling between 1965 and 1999 (one review); no rise in a British general-practice study (cited to a 2008 government report) and no change or a decrease in diagnosed schizophrenia in the UK from 1996 to 2005 (a 2009 paper cited by another review); at least a tenfold rise in UK cannabis use since the 1970s (from a commentary) without a rise in first admissions (no source given). Across 10 sites: correlation of adjusted incidence with daily use among controls r = 0.8 (p = 0.0109) and with high-potency use r = 0.7 (p = 0.0286); the two exposures correlate across sites at about 0.71 by the editors' calculation from the site table, although the paper prints r = 0.2.

evidence.locator: Cannabis and mental health, 3rd paragraph (right column, p. 1388); references 88 to 92 (p. 1391)
evidence.extracted: Evidence is called conflicting on whether schizophrenia incidence rises as cannabis use rises in young adults, as a causal association would predict: an Australian study (ref. 88, the authors' own group) did not show clear evidence of increased psychosis incidence despite steep rises in cannabis use in the 1980s and 1990s; a similar study (ref. 89) suggested it was too early to see any increase in England and Wales in the 1990s; a British (ref. 90) and a Swiss (ref. 91) study reported increases in the incidence of psychoses in recent birth cohorts, but another British study failed to do so (ref. 92). By the reference list, ref. 90 concerns south-east London between 1965 and 1999, ref. 91 the incidence of psychotic disorders among the young in Zurich, and ref. 92 is a 2008 report of the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs. Second-hand.

The evidence on trends in schizophrenia incidence is called mixed: no increased psychosis incidence in an Australian modelling study after steep rises in use (ref. 98); too early to detect an increase in a British modelling study (ref. 99); increased incidence of psychoses in recent birth cohorts in case-register studies in Britain (ref. 100) and Switzerland (ref. 101); no increase in a British study of people treated for schizophrenia in general practice (ref. 90, the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs). The author argues that even a causal effect would produce a very modest increase in incidence, and that changes in diagnostic criteria and services, poor administrative data and possible falls in incidence from social improvements such as antenatal care complicate detection. Second-hand.

evidence.locator: Evidence inconsistent with a causal relationship (single paragraph)
evidence.extracted: Some studies found that incidence of psychotic outcomes increased in recent decades (refs 58, 59), others no change or a decrease (refs 60, 61); the authors call such ecological evidence only very weak evidence for causality, because it cannot show that the people using cannabis are those developing psychosis, cannot account for confounders, and does not account for other risk factors that may have declined over the same period. The first reader found that two of the four references (58 and 60) do not concern incidence over time by their titles, leaving one trend study each way (59 and 61).

evidence.locator: Literature Review › 8. Experiment, 1st paragraph (p. 8) and 2nd paragraph (pp. 8-9)
evidence.extracted: Citing a commentary by Gage et al. (ref. 2): at least a 10-fold increase in UK cannabis use since the 1970s, while data on first admissions for schizophrenia show no increase, and perhaps a slight decrease, over that time; UK hospital admissions for cannabis psychosis fell after the 2004 relaxation of cannabis regulation and rose after the return to stricter classification in 2009, although the authors doubt the changes affected use much. Second-hand.

evidence.locator: CRITICISMS OF THE CAUSAL HYPOTHESIS, 1st to 5th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: As argued by the review: reliable information on incidence trends is scarce; what the authors call the only competent long-term study using the same criteria found that the incidence of schizophrenia doubled between 1965 and 1999 in south-east London and that the proportion of patients who had used cannabis rose disproportionately (Boydell et al., 2006). No study reporting stable incidence is cited.

evidence.source_read: PMC full text PMC5032490 (World Psychiatry 15(3):195-204; all sections and Table 1 read)

evidence.extracted: Projected trends for schizophrenia incidence have not paralleled trends in cannabis use over time (ref. 60), which has been used as an argument against causal effects; other projections suggest that time lags and a lack of reliable incidence data mean changes in schizophrenia incidence may not yet be fully apparent (ref. 61). Cited, not analysed, in this review.

Across sites, adjusted incidence of psychotic disorder (from the EU-GEI incidence study) correlated with the prevalence among controls of daily use (r = 0.8, p = 0.0109) and of high-potency use (r = 0.7, p = 0.0286); London (daily use in 26 of 223 controls) had 45.7 cases per 100,000 person-years and Bologna (3 of 65) 21.0. Figure 3 plots 10 sites; the printed p-values fit r of about 0.76 and 0.69, and the first reader found the two site-level exposures strongly correlated with each other (about 0.71), against the r = 0.2 printed.

evidence.locator: Evidence inconsistent with a causal relationship, single paragraph (AM p. 11); References 58 to 61 (AM p. 17)
evidence.extracted: Among studies finding no change or a decrease in the incidence of psychotic outcomes the review cites ref. 61, Frisher et al. (2009, Schizophrenia Research), on the impact of cannabis use on trends in diagnosed schizophrenia in the United Kingdom from 1996 to 2005, a published paper; among studies finding increases, ref. 59, Boydell et al. (2003), on the incidence of schizophrenia in south-east London between 1965 and 1997 (refs 58 and 60 do not concern trends by their titles). The review gives as reasons for calling such evidence weak the ecological fallacy, unaccounted confounders and other risk factors that may have declined; it does not discuss diagnostic or service changes.

evidence.locator: Discussion, paragraph on projected trends (p. 326); References 60 and 61 (p. 328)
evidence.extracted: The review cites, without analysing them, two projections of schizophrenia trends: ref. 60, Degenhardt, Hall and Lynskey (2003), and ref. 61, Hickman et al. (2007), model projections for England and Wales. By authors, year and title these are the Australian and British modelling studies that Hall and Degenhardt (2009, refs 88 and 89) and Hall (2015, refs 98 and 99) cite (editors' cross-check of the reference lists).

Only the rise in UK cannabis use, at least tenfold since the 1970s, is attributed to Gage et al. (ref. 2); the statement that data on first admissions for schizophrenia show no increase, and perhaps a slight decrease, over that time carries no citation.

risk_of_bias.note: Ecological designs: modelling studies and treated or registered cases, which cannot link any person's use to their illness or account for confounders and other changing risk factors (Gage et al., 2016); the UK admissions figure has no stated source; the site comparison rests on 10 points and two strongly correlated exposures (card sc_di_forti_2019).

inconsistency.note: The studies point in different directions (no rise in Australia and in UK first admissions; rises in south-east London and Zurich), with explanations offered (time lags, diagnostic and service changes) but not tested.

indirectness.note: Every time-trend figure is second-hand, from narrative reviews and one commentary not read; trends in treated or admitted cases are a distant measure of population incidence and of the causal question.

imprecision.note: No estimates with intervals are given for the time trends; not rated separately.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; the reviews cite a small, selected set of trend studies.

grade.reasoning: Observational, starts low; down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness: very low. Every anchor that supports the time-trend statements cites a narrative review, so the figures are second-hand and the claim stays at draft (METHODS §6.3). Counted once: Hall & Degenhardt (2009) and Hall (2015) cite the same trend studies, and Moore et al. (2007) cite two of them; the 10-site correlation is a different comparison (across places, not over time) and qualifies the claim rather than answering it. Status mixed: several studies with inconsistent findings and no adequate explanation of the differences.
